site.title: Octos | Rust agent runtime
site.description: Octos is a Rust runtime for agent tasks. Embed its crates or connect over OUP to run turns, tools, context management, memory, and model routing.

footer.brandDescription: Rust runtime for agent tasks. Embed the crates or connect to an Octos host over OUP.
footer.license: Open source under the Apache License 2.0.
footer.ownership: Official deployments: www.octosai.org and learn.pitun.cc — operated by the octos-org maintainers.

hero.heading:
Embeddable
agent runtime
hero.description: Octos runs agent turns, tool calls, context management, memory, and model routing. Embed the Rust crates, use a native binding, or connect to a host over the Octos UI Protocol (OUP).

items.title: Turns and sessions
items.description: Open, hydrate, fork, roll back, and compact sessions. Start, steer, or interrupt a turn. The runtime stores the transcript, execution state, and event order.

items.title: Context compaction
items.description: A preflight token check can prune old tool output or run a compaction pass before the next model call.

items.title: Persistent memory
items.description: Task episodes, Markdown notes, and entity records are stored separately. Retrieval combines keyword and vector search.

items.title: Tool execution
items.description: Built-in tools cover shell commands, file edits, search, web access, Git, and delegation. Sessions can also register MCP and plugin tools.

items.title: Model routing
items.description: Select a provider and model directly, or route by capability. Retry, failover, hedging, and circuit breakers handle provider failures.

items.title: Agent delegation
items.description: Run a child agent within a turn, assign work to a peer with its own session, or dispatch a validated swarm job.

items.title: Sandbox and permissions
items.description: Permission profiles limit filesystem and network access. Platform sandbox backends enforce the selected profile where available.

items.title: Lifecycle hooks
items.description: Shell hooks run at defined lifecycle points. A before-hook can reject an action; repeatedly failing hooks are disabled.

items.title: Scheduled execution
items.description: Goals, loops, and monitors can schedule continuation turns. Token budgets and stop conditions bound their execution.

architecture.label: Architecture
architecture.heading: Runtime components and interfaces
architecture.description: The Rust workspace separates protocol types, agent execution, sessions, model access, and memory. Applications can call the crates in process or use OUP over stdio or WebSocket.

protocol.label: Protocol
protocol.heading:
OUP methods
and transports
protocol.description: OUP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 for session operations, turns, approvals, and events. Clients negotiate supported features when they connect and can resume a session from an event cursor.

transports.name: WebSocket
transports.description: The /api/ui-protocol/ws endpoint carries client requests and runtime events over WebSocket.

transports.name: stdio
transports.description: octos serve --stdio exchanges one JSON object per line; protocol data goes to stdout and logs to stderr.

transports.name: In-process
transports.description: Native clients can call the dispatcher within the same process.

protocol.code: // start a turn {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"req-turn-start","method":"turn/start", "params":{"session_id":"local:demo","turn_id":"<uuid>", "input":[{"kind":"text","text":"hello"}]}} // approve a tool call the agent asked about {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"req-approval","method":"approval/respond", "params":{"session_id":"local:demo","approval_id":"<uuid>", "decision":"approve"}} // resume after a disconnect {"stream":"events","seq":42}
protocol.note: The runtime streams message and tool updates as notifications. Durable events are recorded before delivery. After reconnecting, a client can request events from its last cursor; if the cursor has expired, it must hydrate the session again.

embedding.label: Embedding
embedding.heading: Integration options
embedding.description: Use the Rust crates directly, call the C ABI, generate Swift or Kotlin bindings with UniFFI, or connect to a running Octos host over OUP.

targets.name: Rust
targets.description: Link the runtime crates into a Rust application.

targets.name: C ABI
targets.description: Use the bundled header to create a runtime, execute a task, and read errors.

targets.name: Mobile
targets.description: Generate Kotlin and Swift bindings with UniFFI.

targets.name: Python
targets.description: Use the native Python extension for scripts and backend integrations.

targets.name: Browser
targets.description: Use WASM protocol and utility types in a web client; the agent runtime runs in a native host.

embedding.code: // C ABI #include "octos.h" OctosRuntime *rt = octos_runtime_new(config_json); char *out = octos_run_task(rt, "{\"prompt\":\"summarize ./README.md\"}"); if (!out) fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", octos_last_error()); octos_string_free(out); octos_runtime_free(rt);

context.label: Context
context.heading: Context compaction
context.description: Before a model call, the runtime checks the token budget and can reduce older context. Clients receive lifecycle events that report when compaction occurs.

features.label: Tier 1
features.description: Prune stale or oversized tool results between iterations while preserving prompt cache prefixes.

features.label: Tier 2
features.description: Use provider-side clearing when the model API supports it.

features.label: Tier 3
features.description: Run extractive compaction or an LLM summary, retaining named artifacts and constraints.

lifecycle.name: hydrate
lifecycle.description: Load a session snapshot and its event cursor into a client.

lifecycle.name: fork
lifecycle.description: Create a branch from a session with selected recent turns.

lifecycle.name: rollback
lifecycle.description: Record an idempotent rollback marker for recent user turns.

lifecycle.name: compact
lifecycle.description: Compact on request or when the token preflight check requires it.

context.note: Pruned tool results retain their call IDs in typed placeholders. With context.lifecycle.v1 enabled, clients receive compaction_started, compaction_completed, and normalization_reported events with triggers and token counts.

memory.label: Memory
memory.heading: Memory stores and retrieval
memory.description: Octos stores task episodes, Markdown notes, and entity records separately. Each has its own write and retrieval path.

layers.title: Task episodes
layers.description: Completed tasks record their outcome, changed files, and decisions in an embedded key-value store. Retrieval selects relevant records for the current workspace.

layers.title: Markdown notes
layers.description: MEMORY.md and daily notes use stable entry IDs and an injection budget. Background jobs capture and consolidate notes.

layers.title: Entity records
layers.description: save_memory writes records for people, projects, and systems. recall_memory retrieves the full record when needed.

toolSystem.label: Tools
toolSystem.heading: Tool registration and execution
toolSystem.description: Tools declare JSON schemas and concurrency requirements. Permission checks run before dispatch; read-only calls can execute in parallel while exclusive calls run in order.

tiers.label: built-in tools
tiers.description: Registered through the built-in tool registry.

tiers.label: concurrency classes
tiers.description: Parallel-safe calls can overlap; exclusive calls execute serially.

tiers.label: tool source files
tiers.description: MCP and plugin tools can be registered at runtime.

providers.label: Models
providers.heading: Provider routing and failover
providers.description: Specify a provider and model, or select a capability lane. The router supports backoff, ordered failover, circuit breakers, and optional hedged requests. OpenAI-compatible local endpoints can run without a cloud API key.

agents.label: Multi-agent
agents.heading:
Sub-agents, peers,
swarm, and fleet
agents.description: Octos supports four execution patterns: child agents within a turn, peer sessions, swarm dispatch for bounded jobs, and fleet workers for durable plans.

modes.name: Sub-agents
modes.summary: A child agent runs under the parent turn and returns a result to the parent.
points: Inherits the workspace, tool policy and sandbox
Cannot re-delegate, spawn or message the user
Depth capped at two, with a typed budget error
spawn_agent starts a child without blocking the parent turn

modes.name: Peer agents
modes.summary: A named peer has its own session, history, model selection, and worktree.
points: Prepared by the runtime, then opened by the client
Uses a separate Git workspace to limit file conflicts
Exchanges work through a file blackboard and explicit gather

modes.name: Swarm and fleet
modes.summary: Swarm dispatch handles bounded fan-out; fleet workers execute persistent plans.
points: Parallel, sequential, pipeline and fan-out topologies
Workers get least-privilege grants: no network unless granted
Blocked workers report status to the supervisor

flow.caption: A master agent delegates work to sub-agents, peers, swarm jobs, and fleet workers, then gathers their results into the goal ledger.

master.name: MASTER AGENT
master.description: Owns the goal and coordinates work

branches.name: SUB-AGENT
branches.description: Bounded work within the parent turn

branches.name: FLEET WORKER
branches.description: Executes part of a durable plan

gather.name: GATHER & VERIFY
gather.description: Collect results and check the work

result.name: GOAL LEDGER
result.description: Record the outcome and next step

loops.label: Automation
loops.heading: Goals, loops, and monitors
loops.description: Goals track a token budget and status. Loops schedule continuation turns; monitors can trigger a turn when a probe detects a change.

stages.name: Goal
stages.description: An objective with a token budget and persisted status.

stages.name: Loop
stages.description: A stored prompt and schedule that enqueue continuation turns.

stages.name: Monitor
stages.description: A probe that starts a turn when its filtered output changes.

stages.name: Stop
stages.description: Budget limits, flood control, and repeated empty turns stop or pause execution.

loops.note: Loop and monitor definitions persist across restarts. Running child processes do not resume automatically. Duplicate continuation requests are coalesced.

security.label: Security
security.heading: Sandbox and permission controls
security.description: The selected permission profile sets allowed filesystem and network access. The host applies a platform sandbox backend when available and reports when enforcement is absent.

layers.title: Six sandbox backends
layers.description: Supported backends include bwrap, Landlock, macOS sandbox-exec, Docker, and Windows AppContainer; a no-sandbox mode is also available.

layers.title: Permission profiles
layers.description: Profiles include read-only, workspace-write, and full access. Full access depends on the runtime mode and an explicit grant.

layers.title: Approval binding
layers.description: An approval is bound to a digest of the tool arguments, its originating room, and the eligible approvers. A consumed approval cannot be reused.

layers.title: Hooks with a circuit breaker
layers.description: A before-hook can deny a tool call. Repeatedly failing hooks are disabled by a circuit breaker.

layers.title: Network policy
layers.description: Cloud and tenant deployments can disable network access by default. --no-network disables it explicitly.

layers.title: Loop and input guards
layers.description: Repeated tool calls can terminate a turn. Fetches are checked for SSRF; hook and probe environments are sanitized.

surfaces.label: Clients
surfaces.heading: Clients and gateways
surfaces.description: Clients use OUP over stdio, WebSocket, or an in-process dispatcher. The gateway connects messaging channels to the runtime.

clients.name: Octoscode · TUI
clients.description: Terminal client that provisions a local runtime and connects over stdio.

clients.name: Octoscode Web
clients.description: Static browser client that connects to octos serve over WebSocket.

clients.name: OctoSense
clients.description: Desktop and mobile shell with an embedded Octos runtime.

clients.name: MCP
clients.description: Octos can connect to MCP servers and expose tools through its own MCP server.

surfaces.channelsNote: The gateway receives messages from configured chat platforms and routes them to sessions.

useCases.label: Integrations
useCases.heading: Integration examples
useCases.description: Octoscode, Octoscode Web, and OctoSense use the same agent runtime through different hosts and transports. These implementations show where the client ends and Octos takes over.

items.title: Octoscode · terminal
items.description: On first launch, the terminal client provisions a compatible Octos binary and starts it over stdio. OUP carries session and turn requests, streamed output, tool events, and approval decisions. The terminal presents navigation and diffs; Octos executes the agent and stores session state.

items.title: Octoscode Web · browser
items.description: The React client connects to a running octos serve over WebSocket. It opens workspaces and sessions, renders tool output and approvals, and hydrates session state after reconnecting. The browser and terminal can attach to the same server session.

items.title: OctoSense · native shell
items.description: The Makepad shell hosts AppCard as a native module. On Android, AppCard can start a bundled Octos binary over stdio; without that binary, it can connect over WebSocket. The card UI handles interaction while Octos handles agent requests and session state.

quickStart.label: Get Started
quickStart.heading: Build and run Octos
quickStart.description: From the Octos repository, install the CLI, initialize a profile, and start a local runtime. The same binary provides the stdio and WebSocket OUP transports.
quickStart.code: # Build and install the CLI cargo install --path crates/octos-cli # First run: profile, provider, model octos init export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key # Start a terminal session octos chat # Serve the protocol on 127.0.0.1:50080 octos serve # Start the stdio JSON-RPC host octos serve --stdio # Serve Octos tools over MCP octos mcp-serve # Check the environment octos doctor

items.question: Which part of Octos do I integrate?
items.answer: For an in-process Rust integration, use the workspace crates. For C, Python, Swift, or Kotlin, use the bindings. If the runtime should run as a separate process, connect to octos serve through OUP.

items.question: What is OUP?
items.answer: OUP is the Octos UI Protocol, a JSON-RPC 2.0 interface over WebSocket, stdio, or an in-process dispatcher. It covers sessions, turns, approvals, and runtime events. Event cursors support reconnect and replay.

items.question: How do I embed it in my app?
items.answer: Use the Rust crates directly, call the C ABI, or use the Python and UniFFI bindings. The Embedding section lists the available interfaces.

items.question: Which models can it use?
items.answer: Octos supports cloud providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, and DeepSeek, plus local OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as Ollama and vLLM. Model routing can retry, fail over, or hedge requests.

items.question: How are tool calls restricted?
items.answer: Permission profiles control filesystem and network access. Platform sandboxes enforce those restrictions where available. Tool calls can require approval, and hooks can deny an action before execution.

items.question: Can a task continue without an active client?
items.answer: Goals track a token budget. Loops schedule continuation turns, and monitors can trigger turns when probes detect a change. Budgets and stop conditions bound execution.

items.question: Is it open source?
items.answer: Yes. The source is available at octos-org/octos under Apache License 2.0.
